shape: 2000 units = 100 executions x 20 independent Python script tasks held in one io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.Parallel block (no per-task or per-flow concurrency limit set, so the worker thread pool is the only throttle)

notes.process_sleep: 2000 units as 100 executions of a flow whose single io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.Parallel task holds 20 independent Python script tasks (task body: time.sleep(0.1)), run on io.kestra.plugin.core.runner.Process. All 100 executions of a rep are POSTed before polling starts (submit_s per rep), so every unit is enqueued in the first ~0.7s of a ~14.5s span; Parallel creates all 20 task runs of an execution at once, so the runnable queue is never empty and the 20 worker threads are the only throttle. span_s is last SUCCESS minus first RUNNING across all 2000 task runs, read from each execution's taskRunList[].state.histories. 2000 units in a SINGLE execution does not work: see kestra_runtime.json execution_size_sensitivity.
notes.process_cpu: Same shape and runner as process/sleep, task body is naive recursive fibo(31). Each task is its own OS process under io.kestra.plugin.core.runner.Process, so the 20 concurrent tasks get 20 real cores on the 32-vCPU box.
notes.docker_sleep: Same shape and workload as process/sleep but on Kestra's stock task runner for script tasks, io.kestra.plugin.scripts.runner.docker.Docker with containerImage python:slim, which creates a volume and a container per task and removes both afterwards. Second data point for what container-per-task costs at concurrency. Concurrency is still exactly 20; the worker threads are simply blocked waiting on the single Docker daemon. Compare the per-task window (RUNNING -> SUCCESS) against the serial container lifecycle measured on the same box, in kestra_runtime.json serial_docker_baseline.
